children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is a structured review of how artificial intelligence tools are approved, deployed, and supervised across an investment organization.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing is the practice of checking whether credit decisions, pricing, marketing, and servicing treat applicants and borrowers fairly regardless of protected characteristics such as race, ethnicity, sex, age, or national origin.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information covers the rules and practices that keep confidential, price-sensitive facts about a company or its securities from being used in trading.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced means checking the output of an AI system against the purpose it was meant to serve, the sources it relied on, and the rules that apply to its use.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk is the work of making AI use accountable to clients, regulators, and the firm's own duties of care and loyalty. In practice, AI now screens loan applications, drafts client communications, flags suspicious transactions, summarizes research, and writes code, so the governance question is not whether models are clever but whether their outputs can be checked, explained, and defended. Investment firms run enablement audits to see which teams use AI, what data those tools touch, and whether controls exist before deployment. Fair lending testing uses statistical methods to compare approval and pricing outcomes across protected groups. Data loss prevention systems watch prompts and outputs for material non-public information. Verification work samples model output against source documents, calculations, and policy rules.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature: access controls, retention rules, and basic model inventories are common in regulated firms, and fair lending testing has decades of precedent in credit underwriting. Other parts remain hard. Large language models are probabilistic, their reasoning is not fully inspectable, and an explanation that satisfies a regulator may not match the model's actual internal process. Bias testing can find disparate impact but cannot prove its cause or predict every edge case, while data loss prevention struggles with paraphrased secrets and legitimate use of sensitive information. The site tracks 149 active AI lawsuits and 222 compliance and regulation pages, which shows how quickly the legal and regulatory perimeter is moving. Verification of AI output is still largely manual, sampling based, and dependent on the quality of the source record.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms gives the reader a starting point for inventory, ownership, and control gaps across a firm. Fair Lending and Bias Testing goes deeper into statistical testing, documentation, and the limits of outcome based review. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients covers model cards, feature attribution, and the difference between a useful narrative and a true mechanistic account. Protecting Material Non-Public Information connects governance to data handling, prompt hygiene, and surveillance of AI tools. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop with review procedures for citations, calculations, and factual claims. Together these pages move from firm wide enablement to specific fiduciary duties, then to the evidence a reader would need to defend a decision.
